newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Unions urge SPD to submit tax reform package.
newsitem.headline: German Unions urge SPD to submit tax reform package.

text.p: Germany's Social Democrats were urged by trade union allies on Wednesday to present concrete alternative proposals to the government's tax reform plan that unions have rejected as unfair to workers.

Roland Issen, chairman of the DAG white collar trade union, said the SPD should quickly put forth a complete package of tax reform proposals instead of just making suggestions on various individual aspects.

"If the SPD is demanding a tax reform that won't increase the size of the deficit and yet at the same time reduce the burden on workers, then they also should put forth suggestions on how they will finance it," Issen told Reuters.
SPD spokeswoman Dagmar Wiebusch said the party had already presented its proposals in the autumn.

Issen's comments came a day before Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who has been away on his annual Easter holiday, is scheduled to give an interview with German television from the Austrian resort town of Bad Hofgastein.

There has been speculation that Kohl will address the stalled efforts to strike a deal on tax reform with the opposition Social Democrats, whose help is needed to ensure the measures pass the SPD-controlled upper house of parliament.
An Easter deadline set by the Bonn coalition to reach a compromise on tax reforms with the SPD expired with no deal -- and not even talks -- in sight.

The coalition has already introduced its 1998 tax bill into parliament, which would cut the main corporate tax rate to 40 percent from 47 percent and cut two points off the 7.5 percent solidarity surcharge on income tax bills levied to aid eastern Germany.
The real row centres, however, on big income tax cuts which would come in a second round of coalition legislation for 1999.
The SPD opposes plans to cut top-rate income tax, wants a drop in income tax for ordinary workers from 1998 and wants Germany's high labour insurance to be slashed this summer.
Union leaders held a meeting on Tuesday and officials said some were not satisfied with the SPD's tactics. Several union leaders said they want the SPD to strike a deal soon with the coalition.
Issen said that the SPD has to make clear how it will finance the tax breaks it wants to give to lower income workers and families.
"Even SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine has said he sees on this point a need to take action and promised to put forth a balanced plan soon," Issen said.

The SPD has insisted on a meeting between Lafontaine and Kohl to break the impasse. SPD party manager Franz Muentefering told German Radio that before the meeting takes place, Kohl will have to explain how he plans to reduce a deficit caused by his reform plans of between 56 and 65 billion marks.
"Otherwise there will be no possibility for tax negotiations," he said. ($ = 1.670 German Marks)
